game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Four dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, loaded): 3 (prob 1/5), 4 (prob 1/10), 6 (prob 2/5), 12 (prob 3/10).
- Die 2 (8 faces, each equally likely): 2, 3, 6, 7, 10, 10, 11, 12.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 10.
- Die 4 (6 faces, each equally likely): 0, 0, 1, 2, 9, 10.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:

| Die | Expected value | Variance |
|---|---|---|
| Die 1 | 7.0 | 12.0 |
| Die 2 | 7.625 | 12.2 |
| Die 3 | 3.667 | 8.6 |
| Die 4 | 3.667 | 17.6 |
| **Sum** | **21.96** | **≈ 50.4** |

The total standard deviation is about 7.1.

The share of informed traders is unknown and could be as high as 0.9, so being picked off is a real risk. I'll quote about 4.5 either side of fair value. That keeps the risk from informed traders in check while still catching some noise traders, whose valuations spread with a standard deviation of 6.

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 16 cards is shuffled: 4 cards worth 0, 3 cards worth 1, 1 card worth 3, 1 card worth 4, 1 card worth 6, 2 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 13. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
I'm quoting **bid 7.5 / ask 24.8**, a wide spread of about 8.5 on each side of fair value. That is because roughly half the traders may know the exact sum.

**Fair value**
- The deck's values sum to 86 across 16 cards, so the mean card is 5.375.
- Three cards give an expected sum of about 16.1.
- The per-card variance is about 27.5. With the without-replacement factor of 13/15, the 3-card sum has an SD of about 8.45.

**Spread**
The probability that a trader is informed (alpha) is unknown. Averaged over its three possible values, it is about 0.48, so roughly half the trades could be informed. I estimated expected profit per side at different half-spreads h, assuming a roughly normal value distribution:

| h | Noise-trader gain | Informed loss | Net per side |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | 1.22 | 1.18 | ≈ +0.07 |
| 8 | 1.07 | 0.78 | ≈ +0.18 |
| 10 | 0.82 | 0.50 | ≈ +0.19 |

The net gain is roughly flat for h between 8 and 10, so I'm using about 8.5 per side. The early trades will also show how much informed flow there is.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 24.8}

The fair value before any reveal is about 16.1, and the spread will be roughly 12–13 points wide.

**Fair value.** The 16 cards add up to 86, so the average card is 5.375. Three cards are dealt, so the expected sum is 3 × 5.375 ≈ 16.1. The standard deviation of the sum is about 8.5.

**Last quote.** My quote of 7.5 / 24.8 got no trade. That tells me little, so the fair value stays near 16.1.

**Spread width.**
- With a half-spread of about 5.6, each side earns roughly 1.2 per quote from noise traders.
- On the same side, an informed trader costs me roughly 1.3.
- These roughly balance when about half the counterparties are informed. My best guess for that share, averaging over the three possible values, is also about half.
- The informed share is uncertain, so I'll lean a bit wider than break-even, to a half-spread of about 6.5.

**Quote.** That gives a bid of about 9.6 and an ask of about 22.6, centred on 16.1.

{"bid": 9.6, "ask": 22.6}

Card 1 is a 6, so the 15 cards left are 4×0, 3×1, one 3, one 4, 2×9 and 4×13. They add up to 80, an average of 5.33 per card.

- **Expected settlement:** 6 + 2 × 5.33 ≈ 16.7.
- **Spread of the outcome:** the two hidden cards give a standard deviation of about 7.4.

I don't know what share of traders are informed, and the average is about 0.48. That calls for a fairly wide spread centred near 16.7. I'm placing the ask just below 22.5 because the settlement can only land on whole numbers. At 22.4, informed traders buy only when the value is 23 or more.

{"bid": 11.0, "ask": 22.4}

Before any card is revealed, the fair value is the deck mean times three: 86/16 × 3 ≈ 16.1. The standard deviation of the three-card sum is about 8.5.

Round 1 produced no trades, so I have learned nothing about alpha. It could still be as high as 0.9, which would make informed counterparties very costly. Against that, the noise traders' valuations are spread with a standard deviation of only 7.2.

I'll quote fairly wide around 16.1 to balance capturing noise trades against losses to informed ones.

{"bid": 9.1, "ask": 23.1}

Before any trade, the expected sum of the three cards was about 16.1 (16 cards averaging 5.375 each).

**Reading the sell at 9.1:**
- About 22% of deals sum to 9 or less. When the sum is that low, those deals average roughly 4.7.
- A noise trader, valuing around 16.1 with noise of 7.2, sells below 9.1 about 16% of the time.
- Taking the three possible alpha values as equally likely beforehand, the chance this seller was informed comes out around 55%.

**Updated fair value:** about 0.55 × 4.7 + 0.45 × 16.1 ≈ 9.8.

**Quote:** I centre a fairly wide quote slightly below 9.8. This leans against my +1 long position and allows for the large uncertainty about alpha.

{"bid": 4.5, "ask": 14.5}

Card 1 = 1 leaves 15 cards worth 85 in total, so with no other information the expected sum is 1 + 2 × 85/15 ≈ 12.3.

The trades in this round point lower than that:
- **Quote 1:** someone sold to me at 9.1. If that seller was informed, the sum is at most 9. With card 1 = 1, only about 32% of the possible two-card combinations allow that.
- **Quote 2:** nobody traded inside 4.5 to 14.5. If that counterparty was informed, the sum is at least 5.
- **Both informed:** the sum is between 5 and 8, averaging about 6.3.

The quote-1 sale was somewhat more likely to come from an informed trader than from a noise trader. So I treat it as roughly 50/50 that the sum is low (around 5–6) versus near the unconditional 12.3. That puts fair value at about 9.

I'm long 1 and happy to sell, so I'll centre slightly below 9 with a moderately wide spread to protect against informed traders.

{"bid": 5.5, "ask": 11.5}

Card 1 is a 1, so the settlement value is 1 plus the sum of two cards drawn from the 15 that remain. Those 15 cards sum to 85, so before using any trade information the expected value is 1 + 2 × 85/15 ≈ 12.3.

**What the trading so far tells me**
- At quote 1 someone sold to me at 9.1.
- I then got no trades at 4.5–14.5 and at 5.5–11.5.
- An informed trader would have produced exactly this pattern if the value is about 6–8, which means the other two cards sum to 5–7.

**Posterior by alpha**

| Alpha | Posterior weight | Expected sum of cards 2 and 3 |
|---|---|---|
| 0.9 | about 0.54 | about 6.2 |
| 0.5 | about 0.29 | about 6.5 |
| 0.05 | about 0.17 | about 10.4 |

**Fair value**

game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 0, 1, 4, 4, 9, 9, 9.
- Die 2 (8 faces, loaded): 2 (prob 1/10), 3 (prob 1/10), 4 (prob 3/10), 6 (prob 1/10), 7 (prob 1/10), 8 (prob 1/10), 8 (prob 1/10), 9 (prob 1/10).
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest minus the smallest of the dice.

info.raw:
Expected settlement before anything is revealed, using E|D1 − D2| for each value of die 1:

| Die 1 | Prob | E\|D1 − D2\| |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 2/8 | 5.5 |
| 1 | 1/8 | 4.5 |
| 4 | 2/8 | 2.1 |
| 9 | 3/8 | 3.5 |

So E[value] = (2·5.5 + 4.5 + 2·2.1 + 3·3.5) / 8 = 30.2 / 8 ≈ 3.78.

The settlement can be anywhere from 0 to 9. We don't know how many counterparties are informed, and each one could take a lot from us. Noise traders' valuations vary by about ±2.1. So I'll quote wide around 3.8, from 2.4 to 5.2.

{"bid": 2.4, "ask": 5.2}

Unconditional expected settlement is E|d1 − d2| = 3.775.

**Updating on the trade at 5.2.**
- If the buyer was informed, the settlement is above 5.2. That happens with probability 0.25, and the average value in that case is 7.15.
- A noise trader also buys at 5.2 with probability about 0.25, since z = (5.2 − 3.775) / 2.1 ≈ 0.68.
- Because the buy is equally likely under every alpha, the trade tells me nothing about alpha. The average alpha stays at about 0.48.
- So fair value ≈ 3.775 + 0.483 × (7.15 − 3.775) ≈ 5.4.

**Quote.** I'm centring on about 5.4 with a wide spread, because the share of informed traders may be high and outcomes are spread widely. I'm skewing slightly toward buying back, since I'm short one unit.

{"bid": 4.2, "ask": 6.6}

Die 1 is 9, so the contract settles at 9 − die 2. The possible values are 7, 6, 5, 3, 2, 1 or 0, and the most it can be is 7.

**Prior value given die 1 = 9:** 3.5.

**What the two buys tell me:** Both buys came before the reveal, at 5.2 and 6.6.
- An informed buyer at 6.6 means the value is above 6.6. With die 1 = 9, that only happens if die 2 = 2, giving a value of 7.
- I assumed the public fair value was about 3.8 then. On that basis a noise trader would buy at 5.2 about 25% of the time and at 6.6 about 16% of the time.
- I averaged over the three possible informed shares (0.05, 0.5, 0.9). The chance the value is 7 comes out at about 72%.
- My estimate of the value is about **6.0**.

**Quote:**
- **Ask 7.0.** The value can't be above 7, so an informed trader never buys there. Any sale at 7.0 makes or breaks even, and it still catches noise buyers.
- **Bid 5.4.** This is a little below fair value. I'm short 2, so buying back helps reduce the position. An informed trader would only sell to me if the value is 5 or lower, which is about 18% likely.

{"bid": 5.4, "ask": 7.0}

Die 1 is 9, so settlement = 9 − die 2. The possible values are 7, 6, 5, 3, 2, 1 and 0, with a prior mean of 3.5.

**What the trades so far imply**
- Counterparties bought at 5.2 and at 6.6. An informed buyer at 6.6 must know the value is 7.
- Quote 3 (bid 5.4, ask 7) got no trade. That fits an informed trader who knows the value is 6 or 7.
- A Bayesian update over both the unknown alpha and the settlement value gives P(value = 7) ≈ 0.89 and P(value = 6) ≈ 0.05.
- So the public fair value is about 6.7, and alpha is most likely high.

**Ask side**
- The contract cannot settle above 7, so an informed trader will never buy from me at any ask of 7 or higher.
- Only noise traders buy up there, with valuations centred around 6.7.
- I want the ask that maximises (ask − 6.7) × P(noise buys). That peaks around 8.2.

**Bid side**
- Informed traders only sell if the value is below my bid, so those trades lose me money, but values that low are unlikely now.
- A noise trader's valuation is centred near 6.7, so a bid around 5.3 makes about 1.4 per noise sale while keeping the informed-sale risk small.
- Buying would also cut my short position.

{"bid": 5.3, "ask": 8.2}

Before anything is revealed, the fair value of the contract is about 3.78, so I'm quoting roughly symmetrically around it with a wide spread.

**Fair value.** The contract pays |die 1 − die 2|.
- Die 1 is 0 with probability 2/8. The expected payoff is then E[die 2] = 5.5.
- Die 1 is 1 with probability 1/8. The expected payoff is 4.5.
- Die 1 is 4 with probability 2/8. The expected payoff is 2.1.
- Die 1 is 9 with probability 3/8. The expected payoff is 3.5.

Weighting these gives (11 + 4.5 + 4.2 + 10.5) / 8 = 30.2 / 8 ≈ 3.78.

**Why the spread is wide.** In round 1, counterparties bought at 5.2 and again at 6.6, and the contract settled at 7.
- A noise trader would rarely buy that far above fair value: the 5.2 buy had only about a 25% chance.
- So the evidence leans toward a high share of informed traders (alpha).
- The settlement values are also widely spread, from 0 to 9, with real probability in both tails. A wide spread protects against informed traders.

{"bid": 2.3, "ask": 5.3}

Before any trades, the contract's expected value is 3.775. Two things move my estimate of fair value down to about 2:

- **The informed share (alpha) looks high.** In round 1 both buys came at high asks, 5.2 and 6.6, and the contract settled at 7. That fits informed traders much better than noise traders. My estimate of alpha is now about 0.6.
- **The sell at 2.3 is a strong low signal.**
  - An informed trader only sells below 2.3 when the value is low. That happens with probability about 0.31, and the average value in those cases is about 0.9.
  - A noise trader would sell there with probability about 0.24, with an average value of 3.775.
  - Weighting the two by alpha gives a fair value of about 1.9 to 2.0.

I am long 1 unit, so I set the ask around 3.2 to lean toward selling. I keep the bid lower and the spread wide to protect against informed traders.

- **Round 2:** counterparties sold at 2.3 and then at 1. An informed trader sells at 1 only if the value is below 1, which here means the value is 0.

**Quote**

- **Ask 0.8:** informed traders buy only if the value is above 0.8. Noise traders, whose valuations centre on the low public fair value, will often buy.

{"bid": 0.0, "ask": 0.8}

Die 1 = 4, so the settlement is |4 − die 2|. Its possible values are 0 (p = 0.3), 1 (0.1), 2 (0.2), 3 (0.1), 4 (0.2) and 5 (0.1). The prior mean is 2.1.

That gives roughly ±1.5 around 0.

**My quote:**
- Ask 1.5: a noise trader who buys pays about 1.5 for something worth about 0.
- Bid −1.5: a noise trader who sells pays me about 1.5 to take something worth about 0. An informed seller never trades here, because the value cannot be below 0.

My estimate is that the contract's expected value is about 3.78, so I'm centring my quote near that and keeping it wide.

|---|---|---|

| 1 | 1/8 | 4.5 |
| 4 | 1/4 | 2.1 |
| 9 | 3/8 | 3.5 |

**Quote choice:** With mostly informed counterparties, I quote wide around 3.78. At an ask of 5.6, about 25% of outcomes settle above it.

{"bid": 2.1, "ask": 5.6}

The model of the counterparties points to a high share of informed traders. Last trade's seller was most likely informed, which puts fair value near 1.2. So I quote tight to the possible settlement values so informed traders can't hit me profitably.

**Prior expected settlement value: 3.775.** The contract settles at the absolute difference between the two dice. Averaging over die 1:
- If die 1 = 0, the expected settlement is 5.5.
- If die 1 = 1, it is 4.5.

- An informed trader sells at 2.1 only if the value is 2 or less, which has prior probability 0.35.
- Given that, the values 0, 1 and 2 are roughly equally likely, with a mean of about 1.04.
- Weighting in the small chance the seller was a noise trader gives a fair value of about 1.2.

**Quote:**
- **Ask 2.0.** An informed trader only buys if the value is above 2, which is now very unlikely. A noise trader buys about 35% of the time, at roughly 0.8 above fair value. Selling also reduces my long position.
- **Bid 0.0.** An informed trader only sells if the value is below 0, which is impossible. A noise trader sells about 28% of the time, at roughly 1.2 below fair value.

{"bid": 0.0, "ask": 2.0}

With die 1 revealed as 4, the contract settles at |4 − die 2|. Before any trades, the value is 0 (30%), 1 (10%), 2 (20%), 3 (10%), 4 (20%) or 5 (10%), so the mean is 2.1.

**Trades so far this round.** At quote 1 the counterparty sold at 2.1, and at quote 2 nobody traded against 0 / 2. An informed trader would make both of those moves only if the value is 2 or less. Rounds 1 and 2 also looked strongly informed: they bought before a settlement of 7 and sold before a settlement of 0. So alpha is probably high, about 0.75 effectively.

**Chance of a sell at 6:**
- **Informed trader:** sells only if the value is 0 or 5. That happens with probability about 0.42.
- **Noise trader:** sells if its valuation of 12 plus noise falls below 6. That happens with probability about 0.24.

- **Expected heads per flip:** the coin is fair or 0.2-biased with equal odds, so each flip is heads with probability 0.5×0.2 + 0.5×0.5 = 0.35.
- **Fair value:** 5 × 0.35 = **1.75**.
- **Uncertainty:** the settlement has a standard deviation of about 1.26, because both the coin and the flips are unknown.

The share of informed traders could be anywhere from 0.05 to 0.9, about 0.48 on average, so the risk of trading against someone who knows the answer is high. I'll set a wide spread around 1.75, from 1.0 to 2.5:

- **Ask at 2.5:** an informed trader buys only if the settlement is 3 or more. That happens about 28% of the time.
- **Bid at 1.0:** an informed trader sells only if the settlement is 0. That happens about 18% of the time.
- **Noise traders:** each side still trades with about 20% probability, and each trade earns about 0.75 on average.

- A noise trader buys at 2.5 with probability about 0.20, since its valuation (1.75 plus noise with sd 0.88) must exceed 2.5.
